1114.title: Dedication
1114.hook: giving away the merit of every practice to all beings
1114.howItsDone: Mahayana communities close a sit, chant or ceremony with a dedication of merit to all beings; in Theravada communities merit is shared too, sometimes while water is poured from one vessel into another as monks recite verses.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the four great vows: beings without number, delusions without end, and a promise made anyway. Your line: numberless, I vow.

Someone has spent an afternoon copying a sutra by hand, line after careful line, the ink still drying. Whatever good came from it, it's theirs. They earned it. And then, before the brush is washed, they give it away. In Mahayana practice, the last words of a session can be words that aren't about the one who practiced at all. They send the good of it out the door, to everyone.
screen: `AN AFTERNOON OF COPYING.` → `THE GOOD IS THEIRS.` → `GIVE IT AWAY.`

segments.voice: Year one met this as sharing the merit; today, the Mahayana turn on it. First, the thing given. Buddhists speak of merit, punya in Sanskrit, puñña in Pali: the good that comes from a good act. Giving, keeping a precept, sitting, chanting, each leaves something behind, like warmth in a room after a fire. The old teaching says good acts bear good fruit; merit is that fruit while it ripens. Second, the turn. In Mahayana practice, merit isn't kept. At the close of a sit or a ceremony, people recite a dedication, turning the merit toward the awakening of all beings. The Sanskrit word is parinamana, often given in English as turning over. The bodhisattva works for all, so even the fruit of the work goes to all. Shantideva's Way of the Bodhisattva closes with a whole chapter of it: may the good of this go here, and there, and to every being in pain. Third, a neighbor in the same house. Theravada Buddhists share merit too. After a meal offered to monks, or a chant for someone who has died, a family may pour water slowly from one vessel into another while the monks recite verses, and the merit is shared with the dead and with all beings. Different words, the same open hand. Fourth, the strange arithmetic. Isn't merit given away lost? Some teachers in this tradition say the opposite: a lamp that lights another lamp isn't dimmed. Either way, the practice ends the session facing outward. The last thought isn't how did I do. It's who else is this for.

segments.voice: Sit for a little while, the way you have on other days, nothing special. Near the end, think of whatever steadiness or quiet this sit gave you, even a little, and send it out: to someone you love, to someone you don't know, to someone having a harder day than you. If you have words from your own tradition for this, say them; if not, the intention is enough.
Dedication. Parinamana, turning the merit of a practice toward all beings, so the good of it doesn't stay with the one who did it. Today's word.
Your line: given away. The good goes out the door, to everyone. See you tomorrow.

1115.title: Why the sutra is honored
1115.hook: in early Mahayana the sutra itself was honored with flowers and incense
1115.carry: where the sutra is opened, a shrine
1115.howItsDone: In Mahayana and Vajrayana communities, sutras are kept wrapped and placed high, lifted with both hands, never set on the floor, and sometimes offered flowers and incense; in Tibetan practice a text may be touched to the forehead before reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dedication: the merit of a practice turned toward all beings before anyone stands up. Your line: given away.

A long bundle, wrapped in cloth, sits on the highest shelf in the room. Nobody puts a cup on it. Nobody sets it on the floor, or steps over it, or tucks it under an arm with the shopping. When it's taken down, it's lifted with both hands, sometimes touched to the forehead first. Inside are loose pages of a sutra. In Tibetan homes and temples, a text like this is handled the way you might handle a sleeping baby. Some of that care has roots in sutras that asked for it themselves.
screen: `A BUNDLE ON THE HIGH SHELF.` → `LIFTED WITH BOTH HANDS.` → `THE SUTRA ASKS FOR IT.`

segments.voice: First, what the sutras say about themselves. The Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines speaks of writing the sutra down as a book, and honoring that book with flowers, incense, scents, garlands and banners. The Lotus Sutra says something similar: wherever it is read, taught or copied, honor it the way you would honor the Buddha. These texts tell you how to treat the page they're written on. Second, the place becomes holy. In the Diamond Sutra, which this path starts reading in three days, the Buddha tells Subhuti that any spot of earth where even a few lines of this teaching are spoken becomes like a shrine for the whole world. Wherever the book is opened, that's the temple. Third, a question scholars ask. Buddhists honor stupas, mounds that hold relics of the Buddha's body. Some scholars have suggested that early Mahayana groups gathered around a written sutra in a similar way, the teaching itself treated as the Buddha's presence. Others think the picture was more mixed. It isn't settled. Fourth, what it changes on a Tuesday. If a book can be holy, reading isn't only taking information in. It's a meeting. You slow down. You wash your hands, maybe. You put the phone face down. The sutras weren't asking people to worship paper. They were asking people to treat the teaching as if someone were present in it, and to let their hands show that before their minds caught up.
screen: `FLOWERS AND INCENSE FOR A BOOK.` · `WHERE IT'S OPENED, A SHRINE.` · `RELICS, OR THE WRITTEN SUTRA?` · `READING AS A MEETING.` · then, large: `THE BOOK HONORED.`

segments.voice: Pick up one book near you that you value, sacred or not, with both hands, and feel its weight, its edges, the texture of the cover. Open it anywhere and read one line slowly, as if someone had written it just for this moment. Then set it down somewhere clean and a little higher than usual, and sit with the line you read.
The book honored. In early Mahayana, the written sutra received flowers, incense and banners, and the place where it was taught became like a shrine. Today's word.
Your line: where the sutra is opened, a shrine. Reading, done this way, can be a meeting. That's today's page.

1116.title: Is it the Buddha's word?
1116.hook: Mahayana sees its sutras as the Buddha's teaching; many Theravada scholars see them as later; both views held in good faith
1116.howItsDone: Mahayana Buddhists study and chant their sutras as the Buddha's teaching; Theravada Buddhists keep the Pali canon as the record of his words, and the two traditions meet and talk across this difference.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the book honored: a sutra lifted with both hands, its reading place made a shrine. Your line: the book honored.

Two monks share a train compartment. One wears the deep red of Tibet, the other the saffron of Sri Lanka. They get talking, and it's friendly, until one of them mentions the Heart Sutra. The other smiles, a little carefully. In his monastery, that sutra isn't part of the canon. To him it's a beautiful later text. To his neighbor, it's the Buddha's word. Neither raises his voice. Neither gets off at the next stop.
screen: `TWO MONKS ON A TRAIN.` → `ONE SUTRA, TWO VIEWS.` → `NOBODY GETS OFF.`

segments.voice: First, what the Mahayana sutras say. They open the way the old discourses do: thus have I heard. The Buddha is there, the monks are there, a question is asked. Mahayana communities receive these sutras as the Buddha's own teaching. Some explain why they surfaced later with a story: tradition says certain sutras were kept safe by the nagas, serpent beings beneath the sea, until someone ready could bring them back. Nagarjuna, the story goes, was that someone. Second, the Theravada view. Theravada keeps the canon in Pali, and the Mahayana sutras aren't in it. There they're read as later works, written after the Buddha's lifetime, sometimes admired, not counted as his words. That's not a sneer. It's a careful view about where a text came from. Third, both sides already had a test. In the Pali Great Passing discourse, the Buddha tells the monks what to do if someone claims, I heard this from the Lord himself: don't accept it and don't reject it; set it beside the discourses and the discipline, and see whether it fits. Some Mahayana writers offered another measure: whatever is well spoken, whatever leads to freedom from suffering, carries the Buddha's word. Fourth, holding it. This path won't settle the question, and doesn't need to. Mahayana Buddhists read their sutras in good faith. Theravada Buddhists keep their canon in good faith. Both views are old, both are argued with care, and both belong to people who bow to the same Buddha. What helps is the skill the monks on the train showed: to hear a view you don't hold all the way to the end, without rushing to win.
screen: `THUS HAVE I HEARD.` · `NOT IN THE PALI CANON.` · `EACH SCHOOL HAS A TEST.` · `HEARD TO THE END.` · then, large: `BOTH HELD IN GOOD FAITH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a question where people you respect disagree, a family decision, a passage of scripture, the right way to do a thing. Let one side speak in your mind in its best, kindest voice, then let the other side speak just as kindly. Don't pick; if you lean, notice the lean, and come back to the breath.
Is it the Buddha's word? Mahayana receives its sutras as his teaching; Theravada reads them as later. Two views, held side by side, ranked by no one here. Today's word.

1117.title: The turn, closed
1117.howItsDone: Mahayana Buddhism is practiced across East Asia, Tibet, the Himalayas and beyond, where people take bodhisattva vows, chant sutras, and honor bodhisattvas such as Guanyin, Manjushri and Ksitigarbha.

segments.voice: Yesterday: is it the Buddha's word? Mahayana receives its sutras as his teaching, Theravada reads them as later. Your line: both held in good faith.

A wagon stops at the side of the road, with room still on board. For three weeks this path has been riding in one: Mahayana, the great vehicle. A vehicle is something that carries, and this name says the carrying is meant for everyone standing at the side of the road. The bodhisattva, the perfections, Buddha-nature, Buddhas in every direction, the great beings with their swords and vows. Today the wagon stops for a moment, so you can look back down the road.
screen: `THE GREAT VEHICLE.` → `ROOM FOR EVERYONE.` → `A LOOK BACK DOWN THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: First, the name and the start. Mahayana, the name this movement gave itself. You met the courtesy that goes with it: call each school by its own name, Theravada for Theravada. And an honest gap: how it began is still debated, and nobody has settled it. Second, the one who carries others. The bodhisattva, who seeks awakening for the sake of all. The six perfections: giving, ethics, patience, effort, meditation, wisdom. The ten grounds, the first one called joy. Under all of it, Buddha-nature, covered but never lost, even in a difficult person. Third, a crowded sky. The Buddha in three bodies. Countless Buddhas in countless worlds. Avalokiteshvara, the one who hears the cries of the world. Manjushri, whose sword cuts through confusion. Samantabhadra and his great vows. Maitreya, the one to come, honored in Theravada too. Ksitigarbha, who goes to the lowest places. And skillful means, the teaching shaped to whoever is listening. Fourth, the book and the vow. The perfection of wisdom, from long sutras down to a single letter, honored as the mother of the Buddhas. The four great vows. Dedication, the good of practice given away. The book honored with flowers. And two views of the Buddha's word, held side by side. Put it all together and one shape shows through: the turn this block traced is a turn outward. Practice isn't only for the one practicing. The vehicle is wide on purpose. Tomorrow the path opens the Diamond Sutra, on an ordinary morning.

The turn. The Mahayana turn outward: bodhisattvas, perfections, Buddha-nature, many Buddhas, a path wide enough for all beings. Today's word.

1118.title: An ordinary morning (section 1)
1118.hook: the Buddha dresses, walks for alms, eats, washes his feet and sits down
1118.howItsDone: The Diamond Sutra is chanted and studied in Mahayana communities, Zen among them; it opens with the Buddha's alms round, meal and quiet sitting.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the turn, closed: three weeks of the Mahayana, a road wide enough for everyone. Your line: the great vehicle.

A man gets up. He gets dressed. He picks up a bowl and walks into town to ask for food. He eats what he's given. He walks back, puts the bowl away, washes his feet, and sits down. That's the whole first section of a great text of the Mahayana. No earthquake, no light from the sky, no gods arriving. Just a morning. For the next stretch of days, this path reads the Diamond Sutra, one short section a day. And it begins, on purpose or not, with chores.
screen: `DRESSED. BOWL. ALMS.` → `EAT. RETURN. WASH. SIT.` → `NO MIRACLE AT ALL.`

segments.voice: First, the name. In Sanskrit the sutra is the Vajracchedika. Max Müller's English translation titled it the Diamond-Cutter; people today call it the Diamond Sutra. A diamond: something hard enough to cut through other hard things. The sutra is going to cut. But not yet. Second, the scene, as the sutra sets it. It opens the old way: thus it was heard. The Buddha is staying near the city of Shravasti, in the Jeta grove, in the garden that Anathapindika gave, with a large company of monks. In the forenoon he puts on his robe, takes his bowl and cloak, and goes into the city for alms. He eats. He comes back from his round. He puts away his bowl and cloak. He washes his feet. He sits on the seat prepared for him, legs crossed, body upright, his attention set before him. Then the monks come and sit nearby. Third, what the sutra doesn't say. No deep thoughts on the walk. Nothing special about the food, nothing holy about the feet. Each act is simply done, then the next, at the speed of a person doing chores. Fourth, why start here. Some readers say this first section is already the whole teaching: before a word of wisdom is spoken, the Buddha shows it, by doing an ordinary morning completely and then sitting down. Others read it as the setting, the way any discourse opens. Either way, a text named for cutting begins with a bowl, a walk, and clean feet.

segments.voice: If you can, do one small chore now, washing a cup, folding a shirt, wiping a counter, the way the sutra tells it: one act, then the next, nothing added. Feel the water's temperature and the weight of the cup, then put the thing away and sit, body upright, attention in front of you. If you can't get up, walk through this morning's first chore in memory, step by step.

1119.title: Subhuti asks (section 2)
1119.hook: how should one set out on the bodhisattva path, and hold the mind?
1119.howItsDone: In monasteries that follow this custom, a monk who asks a teacher a question in assembly rises, arranges the robe over one shoulder, kneels and joins palms, as Subhuti does in the Diamond Sutra; the sutra itself is chanted and studied in Mahayana communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Diamond Sutra opened on an ordinary morning: robe, bowl, alms, a meal, washed feet, a seat. Your line: an ordinary morning.

The Buddha has just sat down. The monks have settled around him. The grove is quiet. Somebody has to go first. Classrooms know this moment: the teacher is ready, the room is full, and nobody wants to be the one to break the silence with a question that might sound foolish. In the Diamond Sutra, one monk stands up. He's an elder, and his name is Subhuti. What he asks is the question the whole sutra will spend itself answering.
screen: `THE ROOM IS QUIET.` → `SOMEBODY HAS TO GO FIRST.` → `ONE MONK STANDS.`

segments.voice: First, how he asks. The sutra slows down to show it. Subhuti rises from his place in the assembly, arranges his upper robe over one shoulder, kneels on his right knee, joins his palms toward the Buddha, and bows. The body asks before the mouth does. Second, what he says first. Not his question. He begins with wonder: how much the bodhisattvas have been helped, he says, how much they've been cared for by the Tathagata. Before he asks for anything, he notices what's already been given. Third, the question itself. Paraphrased: when someone has set out on the bodhisattva path, how should they stand? How should they go on? And how should they hold the mind? Three parts, really one: where do I put my feet, how do I keep walking, and what do I do with this restless thing behind my eyes? It's a beginner's question, and Subhuti is no beginner. That's part of its force: the elder asks it on behalf of everyone who's just starting. Fourth, the answer that isn't one yet. The Buddha says, well said, Subhuti, well said. Listen, and take it well to heart, and I'll tell you. And Subhuti says, so be it, and waits. That's the whole of section two: the question asked, praised, and left hanging in the air overnight. Some readers find a teaching there too: a good question deserves a moment of silence before anyone rushes to answer it.

1120.title: All beings freed, none freed (section 3)
1120.hook: lead all beings to nirvana, yet no being is led, because a bodhisattva has no idea of a self
1120.howItsDone: Section 3 of the Diamond Sutra is chanted and studied in Mahayana communities as a teaching on the bodhisattva vow: to free all beings while holding no idea of a self, a being, a living thing or a person.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Subhuti knelt and asked how one should stand, go on, and hold the mind. Your line: how to hold the mind.

A volunteer at a food bank goes home after a long shift. Somebody asks, how many people did you help today? It's a fair question. There's a clipboard. There's a number. And yet something about the question sits a little wrong, as if the people who came through the line were points on a scoreboard. The Diamond Sutra's first answer to Subhuti goes right at that discomfort. Free every being, it says. And then: no being has been freed.
screen: `HOW MANY DID YOU HELP?` → `A CLIPBOARD, A NUMBER.` → `FREED, AND NONE FREED.`

segments.voice: First, the size of the vow. The Buddha tells Subhuti how one on the bodhisattva path should think. All beings, of every kind: born from an egg, from a womb, from moisture, or appearing all at once; with form or without; with perception, without it, or neither. All of them I must lead into nirvana, the kind that leaves nothing behind. It echoes the first of the four great vows. Second, the cut. Here the diamond comes in: and yet, after leading beings beyond measure to nirvana, no being at all has been led. That isn't a riddle tossed off for effect. It's the sutra's first real move. Third, the reason the text gives. If a bodhisattva held the idea of a being, they couldn't be called a bodhisattva. Nor if they held the idea of a self, or a living thing, or a person. The helper who keeps a tally of the helped has already turned people into things that can be counted, and turned themselves into the one who counts. Fourth, what it isn't saying. It isn't saying don't help. The vow to free all beings stands, at full size. It's saying help without building a self out of the helping. Some readers hear freedom for the helper too: no ledger to keep, no score to defend, no hero in the story. And this week points the same way: merit given away, a book honored, two views held in good faith, a wide vehicle looked back on, a morning done fully, a question asked well.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one good thing you did for someone recently, and notice if a little voice says, that was good of me. Don't fight it; watch it, the way you'd watch a cloud cross a window. Then let the picture change: not me helping them, just help happening, no helper, no helped, no number.
All beings freed. Lead every being to nirvana, the Diamond Sutra says, and yet no being is led, because a bodhisattva holds no idea of a self or a being. Today's word.
